title: Who should own water? Lessons from France and the Netherlands
label: 20 October 2026 · Reforming the water sector
summary: The Committee questioned international experts about how different ownership and regulatory models affect water service quality, investment and public trust. The session compared France’s local-authority-owned, contract-based system and the Netherlands’ public-shareholder companies, explored how each funds long-term investment, and discussed practical lessons for catchment-based planning, local capacity-building and how to finance climate-driven upgrades.

chapters.title: Why the Committee is asking about ownership
chapters.takeaway: The UK has long debates about whether public, private, or mixed ownership best delivers clean water, secure supply and affordable bills.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we focus on ownership and regulation. The Committee has heard many views about privatisation since 1989; we want practical lessons from France and the Netherlands.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: A quick framing question: has privatisation solved the sector’s problems, or do the problems lie with regulation and finance?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: In France the key point is local-government responsibility. Ownership stays public; local councils decide whether to run services themselves or sign concession contracts with private operators.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: In the Netherlands water companies are legally private firms but must be owned by public bodies (municipalities or provinces). That structure aims to combine managerial autonomy with public oversight.

chapters.title: How France organises water services
chapters.takeaway: Local governments own systems, sign contracts with operators for defined services and penalties, and increasingly bring services back in-house where they want direct control.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Marine, can you explain a French concession and its pros and cons in plain terms?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: A concession sets the service standards, length and penalties; the private operator bills users and runs day‑to‑day operations, while the council keeps long‑term investment control.

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: Advantage: councils set priorities and can use private expertise where helpful. Disadvantage: many French utilities are small and lack technical or financial capacity, making it hard to fund big climate adaptation work.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: We saw remunicipalisation in Paris and Montpellier. What drove that?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: Two drivers: public distrust after past opacity and scandals, and a political choice to integrate water with urban planning—keeping control of the whole water cycle for local policy goals.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Practically, how do towns do the takeover?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: First a political decision; then they create a public company (régie), offer jobs to existing staff (French law protects workers), and sometimes outsource parts like billing to the old operator while capacity is built.

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: Early evidence shows public operators can maintain quality and innovate (Montpellier won an EU R&D project). But funding big pipe replacement remains a major worry.

chapters.title: The Dutch approach: public owners, autonomous companies
chapters.takeaway: Dutch utilities are owned by municipalities/provinces but operate as companies; they borrow for investment, tariffs fund costs, and a public bank helps finance major projects.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Klaas, how does the Netherlands’ model work in practice and what are its strengths?

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: Law requires that utilities be run as companies but owned by public bodies. They must guarantee supply and care for infrastructure while shareholders (local authorities) protect public interests, including tariffs.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: Strengths: stable trust, municipal voice in ownership, and access to bank lending at favourable rates. Weaknesses: tariffs are rising as aging infrastructure and new contaminants need work.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: What about the Netherlands Water Bank?

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: It provides low-cost loans for public-purpose projects; water utilities can borrow from it, though it now funds a wider set of social projects. Private banks still lend easily to water utilities because risk is low.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: Because utilities fund themselves mainly through tariffs, affordability is handled via social benefits rather than direct tariff subsidies.

chapters.title: Finance, tariffs and the big investment question
chapters.takeaway: All systems face the same funding problem: climate-driven upgrades and pipe renewals require large sums; whether public or private, money must come from tariffs, borrowing or public funds and local capacity matters.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: France and the Netherlands mostly fund investment through tariffs and loans. Is that sustainable when water use must fall (demand management) and climate risks rise?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: That is France’s dilemma: 'only water pays for water' pushes tariffs up as we sell less water. Local river-basin agencies sometimes redistribute funds, and concessional loans help, but councils lack scale and must merge services.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: In the Netherlands utilities borrow and repay like mortgages; tariffs rise as needed. Public banks and good credit help keep costs down, but replacements and new investments still push tariffs higher.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Is a catchment-based plan the right unit for investment and environmental trade-offs?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: Yes—river-basin or catchment-level agencies can prioritise projects and channel concessional loans. They help target scarce funds where nature-based solutions can replace costly engineering.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: Agreed. The governance and enabling environment around utilities matter more than ownership alone—shared labs, joint procurement, and cross-council boards can raise capacity.

chapters.title: Practical lessons for the UK
chapters.takeaway: There is no single perfect ownership model; the UK should focus on a clear national strategy, stronger and smarter regulation, local catchment planning, building local capacity, and creating low-cost long-term finance.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: If you were advising Ministers: what first steps should the UK take?

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: Strengthen local authorities’ capacity to own or steer services, set clear catchment plans, and use contract design (penalties and incentives) wisely if private operators stay involved.

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: Put regional planning and catchment priorities first, ensure predictable low‑cost finance (public bank or credit mechanisms help), and keep utility governance aligned with public shareholders’ objectives.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Does changing ownership alone fix the problems?

turns.speaker: Professor Schwartz
turns.text: No. Ownership interacts with regulation, finance and local governance; successes in other countries come from that package, not ownership by itself.

turns.speaker: Dr Colon
turns.text: And remember social and political choices matter: remunicipalisation has succeeded politically where councils wanted wider control over water as part of urban policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. The Committee will reflect on these practical options—catchment planning, local capacity, contract design and financing are clear themes to explore further.
